title: Deciding limit cycles
credit: Extension of Graca-Zhong (arXiv:2101.07701) noncomputability of planar periodic orbits; related: Hilbert's 16th problem, Il'yashenko on algebraic unsolvability of the center-focus problem.
results: The claim that hyperbolic limit cycles are r.e. via interval certification is correct. The remark that fixed-degree versions 'can become trivially decidable' is wrong. Each fixed-degree set is still infinite. Bautin's finite generation only gives non-uniform decidability of the local center condition, not of whether cycles exist.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.22058 (2026 preprint): cited only for the claim that the planar (N=2) case is open and that Lyapunov stability is undecidable in dimension 5; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Given a polynomial vector field in the plane with rational coefficients, is there an algorithm that decides whether it has a limit cycle, that is, an isolated closed orbit? Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles there can be. This asks only whether their existence is algorithmically decidable. The same question can be asked for closed orbits of any kind, including those in period annuli around centres.
math: Let $\mathcal L=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:\ \dot x=P,\dot y=Q$ has a limit cycle, i.e. a non-constant periodic orbit that has a neighbourhood containing no other periodic orbit$\}$ and $\mathcal P=\{(P,Q):$ the system has a non-constant periodic orbit in $\mathbb R^2\}$, with inputs given by their rational coefficient lists (degree unbounded). (a) Is $\mathcal L$ decidable? (b) Is $\mathcal P$ decidable? (c) Are $\mathcal L,\mathcal P$ or their complements recursively enumerable? (d) Same questions restricted to degree 2.
